title: E31 - Zach and Richard's Excellent Legal AI Adventure: Robin AI's Struggles and the Future of LegalTech
author: Zach Abramowitz · Richard Tromans

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source contains only a podcast sign-off and offers no substantive claim, evidence or argument about user-led legal AI adoption, automation readiness, verification, market scenarios or skills. Its position relative to the cluster therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s hybrid, lawyer-in-the-loop account: AI-enabled ALSPs deliver legal work rather than merely software, while complex matters still require strong legal teams because AI can add errors. It materially extends the synthesis by showing that provider categories may converge according to the actual human–technology split and by identifying clear service-model positioning as an operational requirement.
qs: And Robin and others, they are selling a work product.

You know, and you start to get to this point where the whole thing starts to blur, and really, you get to a point where some of the only questions are, how far have you got on that dividing line, right?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI should be selectively deployed within expert-led workflows rather than treated as general legal competence. It materially extends the synthesis by distinguishing software vendors from AI-enabled legal-service providers and linking the human–AI division of labour to provider identity, scalability, ROI and market positioning.
qs: The thinking in AI, like the thinking today is, AI plus the very best people.
SPEAKER_2 (00:26:35) But that traps them in doing relatively straightforward, standardized contracts, right?

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core framing by identifying sustained foundation-model pressure on vertical legal-AI vendors while expecting specialist legal technology to persist. It also directly reinforces the distinction between software vendors such as Harvey and providers such as Robin that deliver legal work product, with qualitative claims of substitution for law-firm work.
qs: So to me, it's like I get, I think the application layer companies are going to continue to have a challenge because they are up against companies that are building just phenomenal user experiences, maybe some of the best user experiences that consumers have ever had in tech.
Yes, but they are not selling work product.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that AI-enabled legal delivery requires a distinct service-provider model rather than merely adding AI to existing staffing, and that execution depends on investment, legal expertise and controls against error. Its discussion of differentiated ALSP work streams and competition is qualitative and does not materially extend the cluster’s broader economic or apprenticeship analysis.
qs: And I think that what they should have really been focused on was we are a new paradigm of service provider.
How much investment are we putting into getting these responses perfectly right?

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the proposition that corporate legal departments are increasingly active AI buyers and can redirect selected work away from law firms. Its Robin AI example specifically describes an AI-enabled ALSP selling completed legal work as a faster, cheaper substitute, while treating displacement as case-specific rather than evidence of universal outside-counsel decline. It also supports the cluster’s distinction between buying software and buying delivered legal work.
qs: So it was like direct replacement and it was very easy to justify the spend on Robin inside some of the big companies who they worked with.
And I think in some instances, there were law firms that lost work directly because of Robin.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI can assist legal work without eliminating the need for human expertise. It specifically argues that complex, high-value matters still require skilled lawyers and that combining AI with insufficiently capable staff may not produce reliable substitution. Its claims are hypothetical rather than empirical and do not establish broader staffing outcomes.
qs: And just throw some AI, throw some junior paralegal-type person at it and it's all going to be fine.
And the other side has their very expensive attorney who also may be using AI.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s caution that legal-AI investment momentum does not establish durable returns. Robin AI’s reported layoffs and funding difficulty provide a warning sign, while the source explicitly leaves the wider market implications unresolved rather than claiming either sector-wide failure or continued growth. It does not materially assess concentration or competing vendor models.
qs: And this week, we are talking about a very timely topic, which is Robin AI and the recent layoffs, the news about them not being able to close around the funding, potentially going insolvent.

kp.k: Robin's financial distress is reported, not confirmed insolvency
kp.d: Richard Tromans reports that Robin AI is seeking a buyer or investor after efforts to secure large investment checks fell short, with layoffs earlier in the year and further departures underway. He credits City AM with breaking the sale-listing story and explicitly cautions that Robin's exact financial position is not public. He also corrects Zach Abramowitz's suggestion that CTO departures were layoffs: his understanding is that co-founder James Clough left voluntarily and the second CTO departed for unspecified other reasons.
qs: As I mentioned in the piece, the exact financial position of Robin is not public, right?
yes, they're looking for a buyer, yes, they're looking for an investor because the first effort to get big investors who would sign big checks really didn't work out as planned.
He was not laid off, as far as I understand.

kp.k: Company distress does not establish systemic AI failure
kp.d: Both speakers reject the interpretation of Robin's difficulties as evidence that legal AI is collapsing. Abramowitz cites his knowledge of other companies raising venture funding and argues Robin was not among the most prominent recent market leaders. Tromans regards the issue as primarily localized, while predicting that two or three other companies could encounter funding difficulties as initial cash runs out and investors scrutinize disappointing growth. He presents possible management, competition and technology explanations as speculation, not established causes.
qs: If anything, I know about more companies right now that are raising money from top VCs.
The truth is we simply don't know.
Will there be others? I think there could be two or three more.
As long as, to your point, some of these leading companies don't go nuts and start hiring way too many people, right, and in a way that they can't match on revenue growth, they should be fine, right?

kp.k: Selling software differs fundamentally from selling completed legal work
kp.d: Tromans distinguishes software vendors such as Harvey from Robin and AI-using ALSPs: employing lawyers to improve software does not make a vendor a seller of legal work product. Robin's combination of technology and people instead overlaps with ALSPs, Big Four legal-service arms and law-firm managed services. The distinction concerns what customers buy, rather than simply whether the provider uses AI or employs lawyers.
qs: Yes, but they are not selling work product. That is the fundamental difference.
And Robin and others, they are selling a work product. Right, no different to a law firm. They're doing it slightly differently.

if you took a big UK law firm that has a managed services arm of its own, maybe they've got a bunch of people up in the north of England somewhere, at a lower cost base, and they're using AI tools. What's the difference?

kp.k: Hybrid providers' actual automation shares remain uncertain
kp.d: Abramowitz characterizes Robin's service proposition as 85% technology and 15% human work. Tromans expressly questions whether that split reflects actual delivery, offering hypothetical 50–50 and 20% technology/80% people alternatives. He argues that substantial dependence on internal lawyers makes such businesses harder to distinguish from existing AI-using ALSPs; none of these percentages is established as a measured operational result.
qs: we're going to be able to do 85% of this with tech and 15% of it with our people.
When you said 85%, is it 50-50% actually?
Is it actually 20% by the tech and 80% by the people? We don't know. Like I said, it's speculation, and it would be interesting to find out.

kp.k: Service substitution offers a clearer customer ROI argument
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that Robin's return on investment is easier to articulate than that of an AI assistant because clients can compare the price and speed of completed work with previous outside-counsel or ALSP spending. He says Robin served private-equity and Fortune 500 customers on significant work and believes some law firms directly lost work to it. These are practitioner assertions rather than quantified customer findings.
qs: I think the ROI of a Robin is actually much clearer than the ROI of a Harvey, right?
I used to pay an outside council or an ALSP a certain amount to do this work. I'm now getting this work quicker and less expensive because I'm using Robin.
And I think in some instances, there were law firms that lost work directly because of Robin.

kp.k: Clear positioning must accompany first-mover advantage
kp.d: Abramowitz attributes part of Robin's difficulty to ambiguous positioning between software product and new service-provider model. He views its rebranding as insufficiently substantive and contrasts its messaging with Harvey's. This is his interpretation, not an established causal explanation of Robin's financial problems. He recommends that firms and technology companies pair early entry with a strong brand and a clear account of what they deliver.
qs: They were fence sitting.
On the one hand, they were like, it was like a product, but on the other hand, it wasn't really a product.
There's a huge advantage to being first mover, but only if you pair it with crystal clear messaging and a very strong brand.
And it felt to me like this was a rebrand of mostly logos and colors.

kp.k: Senior legal leaders increasingly shape AI purchasing
kp.d: Abramowitz reports that corporate general counsel and chief legal officers are taking direct interest in AI, whereas previously they often delegated technology attention to legal operations. He also says many law-firm AI-assistant purchasing decisions have come through managing partners rather than experienced technology buyers. His earlier interpretation of Robin's conference absence as evidence of successful direct outreach is explicitly reconsidered: budget constraints could instead explain it.
qs: when you talk to chief legal officers and general councils at major corporations, very often they are interested in AI.
Many of the decisions about which AI personal assistant to buy for the law firm, you know this, have come through managing partners of the law firms.
It's not always that these decisions are being outsourced to an experienced tech buyer.

kp.k: AI-native services optimize turnaround and human review time
kp.d: Abramowitz contrasts established labor-centered service businesses that add technology with AI-native providers designed around process improvement. Using Crosby as an example, he describes objectives of reducing total turnaround time and human review time, aiming to return contracts within an hour with better recommendations at lower cost. He invokes the innovator's dilemma to explain why existing providers may struggle to move away from labor-centered operations. These are descriptions of strategic goals, not demonstrated performance figures.
qs: But I think at their core, the businesses are our body shops. That's how they operate. And it's really hard to move away from that.
And this is like classic innovators dilemma stuff.
And they need to reduce the hurt human review time.
we are just going to build our process until we can give back your contract within an hour of you sending it to us with all of the best recommendations.

kp.k: Complex legal work requires AI plus experienced practitioners
kp.d: Both speakers advocate pairing AI with highly capable lawyers rather than treating it as a substitute for expertise through cheap or inexperienced labor. Tromans distinguishes standardized contract services from more complex work and argues that experienced practitioners must recognize good and bad output and understand the surrounding legal issues. His journalism analogy illustrates how powerful but imperfect AI combined with weak judgment could worsen work product; this is an argument, not a measured comparison of lawyer performance.
qs: AI, do not try to combine AI and cheap people, right? AI and the best.
I think if you're going to do complex contracts, okay, you need good tech, but you also need really good lawyers.
You want a super smart, super experienced person who knows exactly what they're doing, who knows what difference between good and bad is, and AI and knows how to use it.
AI plus inexperience plus the inability to know good from bad is actually a multiplier towards the negative, right?

kp.k: Automation limits and competitive expertise may sustain premium lawyers
kp.d: Tromans argues that aggressive speed and automation targets currently constrain providers toward relatively standardized contracts, while speculating that AI might handle very complex deals in five or six years. Abramowitz is more skeptical that cheap lawyers plus AI will ever displace strong counsel in adversarial dealmaking: if the other side's expensive, skilled lawyer also uses AI, the relative advantage of expertise remains. Neither provides empirical forecasts.
qs: But that traps them in doing relatively straightforward, standardized contracts, right?
maybe in five, six years, AI will just be so incredibly brilliant that we, you know, we can do the most complex deals and contracts and so forth.
It's because the other side has a very expensive smart attorney.
And the other side has their very expensive attorney who also may be using AI. Like, who's going to come out with the better deal terms in that case?

kp.k: Legal application layers supply integration and usability value
kp.d: Tromans defends specialized legal AI applications as more than superficial packaging: data connections, workflows, interfaces and user experience make underlying models usable in legal practice. He argues that most lawyers lack the time, desire or technical ability to assemble tools themselves, and that organizational IT security can prevent such assembly even where skills exist. Abramowitz likewise argues that packaging is itself a difficult and competitive business.
qs: We haven't emphasized what goes into a good application layer, from the data connections to the workflows to the UI to the UX.
how many lawyers in the regular day job world of lawyers, know how to code, want to code, want to smash all these different tools together, can handle it all.
And in fact, even if they did that, would their IT security team internally allow them to do it?
packaging is actually like very, like very difficult and very competitive.

kp.k: Frontier-model interfaces challenge specialized vendors and approved tools
kp.d: Abramowitz reports Harvey leadership's characterization of OpenAI as its biggest competitor and agrees that frontier-model providers' rapidly improving user experiences challenge legal application vendors. He argues that workplace guardrails can make approved AI tools less useful than consumer alternatives, prompting users to move outside firm-approved systems to Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. Tromans nevertheless predicts that law firms will broadly retain legal-specific products, with possible exceptions among small firms and firms pursuing direct technology partnerships.
qs: Open AI is their biggest competitor.
the AI that people are using in their personal life is actually better technology than what they're being given to use at work
so many people will leak very often outside of their current firm approved tool and default back into Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini
I think law firms for one, will stick with legal tech products broadly.

kp.k: Delayed experimentation risks a difficult adoption catch-up
kp.d: Abramowitz recommends simple experimentation across multiple AI options rather than excluding products or doing nothing, arguing that firms should have pursued this over the preceding three years. Tromans says some firms remain nonadopters despite broad uptake and predicts an abrupt need to catch up when client expectations become unavoidable. His reference to 10 out of the top 100 illustrates the significance of a residual nonadopter group; he identifies no particular survey or methodology.
qs: I think what law firms should have been doing over the past three years was experimenting in the simplest ways possible.
They should have been looking at this. And the worst thing that you could have done up until now is nothing.
so 10 out of 100 of the top 100, that's actually quite a significant number.
all of their clients expect them to have this technology and they literally haven't even touched it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Abramowitz and Tromans argue that Robin AI's difficulties do not signal the end of legal AI growth, although Tromans anticipates further company-level troubles.
pts.d: Abramowitz cites his knowledge of other legal-AI companies raising venture capital. Tromans describes Robin's situation as primarily localized and attributes broader market growth to improving models, increasing uptake and increasing revenue. He nevertheless predicts that funding pressure may expose problems at two or three more companies as their runways expire and investors scrutinize growth. These are market assessments and predictions, not quantified sector findings.

pts.k: Abramowitz claims that AI-enabled delivery of completed legal work can offer clearer buyer ROI than legal-assistant software and can directly displace incumbent providers.
pts.d: He contrasts Robin's delivery of work using AI and lawyers with Harvey's sale of software. In his account, corporate buyers can compare Robin's price and turnaround directly with spending on outside counsel or ALSPs. He says Robin served private-equity and Fortune 500 clients and believes some law firms lost work to it. No customer-level cost figures, contracts or measured savings are supplied.

pts.k: Tromans distinguishes AI software vendors from AI-enabled legal-service providers by whether they sell software or completed work product.
pts.d: Tromans says employing lawyers to improve a software product does not make a vendor a legal-work provider. He groups Robin with ALSPs and law-firm managed-service operations insofar as they deliver work product. He suggests the distinction between AI-native providers and established AI-using ALSPs becomes blurred when delivery remains heavily dependent on human lawyers. The actual human/AI division of Robin's work is explicitly unknown; the percentages discussed are hypothetical rather than measured automation rates.

pts.k: Abramowitz argues that first-mover advantage in legal AI depends on clear positioning and a strong brand.
pts.d: He interprets Robin's positioning between software and service delivery as insufficiently clear, and believes its rebrand emphasized appearance rather than its distinctive service model. He contrasts this with Harvey's branding and with providers explicitly positioning themselves as AI-plus-people businesses. This is his retrospective strategic interpretation, not an established explanation of Robin's financial difficulties.

pts.k: Both speakers argue that AI increases the importance of experienced professionals rather than making inexperienced, low-cost personnel adequate for complex legal work.
pts.d: Tromans argues that complex contracts require strong lawyers as well as strong technology, and that inexperienced users unable to distinguish good output from bad may amplify quality problems. Abramowitz contrasts this approach with earlier low-cost outsourcing models. Their support consists of professional reasoning, examples of experienced teams at AI-enabled providers and Tromans's analogy to journalism, not comparative performance tests. The claim concerns augmentation by experienced professionals, not autonomous reliance on AI output.

pts.k: Abramowitz predicts that high-stakes adversarial dealmaking will preserve demand for expensive, highly skilled lawyers even as AI improves.
pts.d: His argument is comparative: a party using a cheap lawyer plus AI would still face a sophisticated opposing lawyer who may also use AI. He therefore rejects the proposition that AI will make the cheaper, less expert combination sufficient in that context. This is an explicitly long-run strategic argument illustrated with M&A negotiations, rather than an empirical finding about prices or staffing.

pts.k: Abramowitz sees AI-native service providers as organized around faster turnaround and less human review; Tromans says this currently confines aggressive automation to standardized work.
pts.d: Abramowitz contrasts firms built around human staffing with Crosby's stated focus on total turnaround time and human review time. He describes returning a contract within an hour as an operating goal, not a demonstrated universal result. Tromans argues that this approach currently fits relatively straightforward contracts and only speculates that the most complex deals might become feasible in five or six years. Neither provides measured turnaround, review-time or quality results.

pts.k: Abramowitz claims AI purchasing is attracting direct attention from senior legal leaders rather than being delegated entirely to technology specialists or legal operations.
pts.d: He reports that general counsel and chief legal officers at major corporations are interested in AI and that managing partners have driven many law-firm AI-assistant purchases. He bases this on his conversations, reports from other companies and Robin's explanation that it prioritized its own events for general counsel. He acknowledges that his earlier favorable interpretation of Robin's absence from a major event may instead have reflected spending constraints.

pts.k: Tromans argues that specialized legal-AI applications add value through integration, workflow and usability, and predicts that law firms will broadly retain legal-tech products.
pts.d: He argues that most practicing lawyers neither want nor know how to assemble tools and code themselves, and that internal IT security may prevent such combinations. He predicts continued use of legal-sector products, while identifying very small firms and firms working closely with general-purpose technology companies as possible exceptions. His support is qualitative reasoning about users, organizational constraints and examples, not adoption forecasts derived from data.

pts.k: Abramowitz predicts sustained competition for legal-AI application vendors from frontier-model companies' own user experiences.
pts.d: He argues that general-purpose AI companies ship strong features and interfaces, while corporate tools can impose restrictions that make them feel less useful. In his account, this leads some users outside approved tools and back to Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. He endorses the competitive concern rather than merely repeating another person's statement. No usage data or comparative product evaluation is supplied.

pts.k: Abramowitz advocates broad experimentation with AI, while Tromans predicts an urgent catch-up problem for non-adopting law firms as client expectations rise.
pts.d: Abramowitz says firms should have experimented over the preceding three years with multiple tools rather than doing nothing. Tromans refers generally to surveys showing a remaining non-adopting minority and predicts a substantial near-term adjustment when these firms recognize client expectations. His reference to ten of the top hundred firms is not accompanied by a named survey, methodology or date and should not be treated as a verified adoption statistic.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode relies predominantly on reporting, industry contacts, professional judgments and company examples, with explicit uncertainty about Robin's financial position and operating model.
pts.d: Tromans credits City AM for reporting Robin's distressed-sale listing and discusses his own reporting on layoffs and fundraising. He cautions that Robin's current financial position is not public, and corrects the suggestion that its CTO departures were layoffs. Neither speaker supplies benchmark results, audited automation ratios, quantified ROI studies or a causal demonstration that branding or staffing choices caused Robin's problems. References to funding at other providers establish examples cited by the speakers, not proof of those providers' operating success.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Predictions range from funding problems in the next few months to speculative automation of complex deals in five or six years; continued growth is conditional on business discipline.
pts.d: Relative dates refer to the 2025 episode. Tromans expects company problems to become visible as initial funding is spent and new rounds are sought. He conditions leading vendors' health on matching hiring to revenue growth. His complex-work automation scenario is tentative, whereas Abramowitz's argument for continued expert-lawyer advantage in adversarial transactions is framed as enduring. The speakers do not provide a fixed date for broad market transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legal-AI vendors, AI-enabled service providers, incumbent law firms and ALSPs, corporate legal buyers, and lawyers with different experience levels.
pts.d: Vendors face fundraising, positioning and platform-competition pressures. AI-enabled providers compete with outside counsel and ALSPs for corporate contract work. Corporate legal departments may obtain faster, cheaper completed work, while senior legal leaders become more directly involved in buying decisions. Experienced lawyers are portrayed as essential complements to AI on complex matters; inexperienced staff are portrayed as vulnerable to quality failures without sufficient expertise. Non-adopting firms face anticipated client pressure. The discussion is primarily about enterprise legal services, not access to justice or unmet civil legal need.
